# Human Performance Benefits of The Automation Transparency Design Principle: Validation and Variation

**Gyrd Skraaning**, Institute for Energy Technology, Halden, Norway, and **Greg A. Jamieson** , University of Toronto, Ontario, Canada

**Objective:** Test the automation transparency design principle using a full-scope nuclear power plant simulator.

**Background:** Automation transparency is a long-held human factors design principle espousing that the responsibilities, capabilities, goals, activities, and/or effects of automation should be directly observable in the human–system interface. The anticipated benefits of transparency include more effective reliance, more appropriate trust, better understanding, and greater user satisfaction. Transparency has enjoyed a recent upsurge in use in the context of human interaction with agent-oriented automation.

**Method:** Three full-scope nuclear power plant simulator studies were conducted with licensed operating crews. In the first two experiments, transparency was implemented for interlocks, controllers, limitations, protections, and automatic programs that operate at the local component level of the plant. In the third experiment, procedure automation assumed control of plant operations and was represented in dedicated agent displays.

**Results:** Results from Experiments 1 and 2 appear to validate the human performance benefits of automation transparency for automation at the component level. However, Experiment 3 failed to replicate these findings for automation that assumed control for executing procedural actions.

**Conclusion:** Automation transparency appears to yield expected benefits for component-level automation, but caution is warranted in generalizing the design principle to agentoriented automation.

**Application:** The automation transparency design principle may offer a powerful means of compensating for the detrimental impacts of hidden automation influence at the component level of complex systems. However, system developers should exercise caution in assuming that the principle extends to agent-oriented automation.

**Keywords:** automation, human–automation interaction, function allocation, supervisory control, trust in automation, display design principles, supervisory displays

## Introduction

The notion that operators of complex technological systems are under-informed by automation has a long history in human factors. Norman (1990) reacted to the ingrained skepticism toward highly automated systems by arguing that “although the human operators are indeed no longer ‘in the loop’, the culprit is not automation, it is the lack of continual feedback and interaction” (p. 8). Billings (1997) captured the variety of aliases this culprit has acquired in the human factors literature:

. . . as automation complexity increases, it becomes more difficult for the designer to provide obvious, unambiguous information about its processes to the monitoring pilot (even if the designer believes that the pilot needs this information and therefore tries to provide it). I call this “opacity.” Others have referred to it as a lack of transparency; the two terms are synonymous in this context. Still others have used the term “lack of feedback” to refer to automation’s failure to communicate effectively with the human operator. (p. 94)

Christoffersen and Woods (2002) characterized the need for feedback from automation as observability. They emphasized that mere availability of feedback is insufficient and call for greater “informativeness”:

. . increases in the complexity and autonomy of machine agents requires a proportionate increase in the feedback they provide to their human partners about their activities. Representations to support this feedback process must emphasize an integrated, dynamic picture of the current situation, agent activities, and how these may evolve in the future. Otherwise, misassessments and miscommunications may persist between the human and machine agents until they become apparent through resulting abnormal behavior in the process being controlled. (Christoffersen & Woods, 2002, p. 6)

The increasing complexity and autonomy of machine agents anticipated by Christoffersen and Woods (2002) is enabled by recent dramatic advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning technologies. A corresponding surge in transparency-related publications posit models of transparency (e.g., Chen et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2014; Lyons, 2013), provide design examples (e.g., Johnson et al., 2014), and report initial empirical evaluations of aspects of those models (e.g., Lyons et al., 2016; Lyons et al., 2017; Mercado et al., 2016; Selkowitz, Lakhmani, Larios, & Chen, 2016; Stowers et al., 2016; Wright, Chen, Barnes, & Hancock, 2016). This swell of interest in transparency in the context of agent-oriented automation anticipates further attention in the human–automation interaction (HAI) literature.

Wickens (2018, p. 39) asserts that automation transparency can compensate for the human performance consequences of high levels of automation. More specifically, the presentation of explicit feedback from automation is assumed to enhance the operators’ understanding of the automation activity, mitigate the loss of situation awareness (SA) associated with high levels of automation, and protect against the damaging effects of automation failures on task performance (see also Trapsilawati, Wickens, Chen, & Xu, 2017). Seong and Bisantz (2008) also conjecture that providing information about automated systems might lead to a deeper understanding of the inner workings of those systems. They anticipate more effective use of (e.g., better decision efficacy in use of a decision aid) and more appropriate trust in the systems when transparency is established. Hoff and Bashir (2015) document the empirical support for transparency as a design feature for creating trustworthy automation.

Although transparency is intended as a generic design principle, it can be expressed differently across domains (and possibly across implementations of automation). Engineering descriptions in process systems focus on the control loop comprised of the plant process, instrumentation, and automation (see dotted orange loop in Figure 1). Historically, the human–system interface (HSI) displays information sensed by the instrumentation and receives control actions targeted at process variables (i.e., the dashed blue loop in Figure 1). Operators are thus expected to infer the state of the automation from indications about the plant process (see Sarter & Woods, 1997).

We can illustrate the transparency principle in the context of the feedback control loop by linking the automation component directly to the HSI (see the solid purple line in Figure 1). In this way, the design principle is expressed as a requirement to make automation activity directly observable to the human operators through the HSI.

We will use the term automation transparency to refer to the design principle that the responsibilities, capabilities, goals, activities, and/or effects of automation should be directly observable in the HSI. (As a shorthand, we will refer to these attributes of automation as automation activity.) Our review of the HAI literature readily leads to the research hypothesis that improved transparency of automation will alleviate or eliminate HAI problems in highly automated systems. In this article, we present three experiments conducted in full-scope nuclear power plant (NPP) simulators with licensed nuclear operators; each of which compared automation displays that were either designed with the transparency principle in mind (i.e., “Transparent”) or adopted traditional design principles for the nuclear power industry (i.e., “Traditional”). Our goal is to test the generalizability of the automation transparency design principle to complex work settings found in safety-critical production systems.

## Experiments 1 AND 2

Experiments 1 and 2 sought to demonstrate the impact of feedback from component-level automation on human performance. Given the minor differences between the methods,

Figure 1. An illustration of the transparent automation principle in process control.

Experiment 2 can be characterized as a replication of Experiment 1. The two experiments are therefore reported together.

## Method

Two full-scope simulator studies tested the human performance of licensed nuclear operators performing realistic control tasks on a familiar nuclear plant.

All experiments reported here complied with the American Psychological Association’s (APA) Code of Ethics and were approved by the Human Participant Protection Committee for Halden Man-Machine Laboratory (HAM-MLAB) experiments. Each participant gave informed consent and had the freedom to withdraw from the study without justification, at any time, and without penalty. The participants were professional nuclear operators and received normal salaries during the data collection.

The reported experiments were among seven HAI studies that the authors reanalyzed and reinterpreted in a technical report prepared for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Halden Reactor Project (Skraaning & Jamieson, 2017), an international center of research excellence for safe and reliable operation of nuclear power facilities (https://ife.no/en/project/the-halden-reactor-project/). Our main contributions were extraction of new findings through complete reanalysis of archival data, discovery of patterns across experiments, and reinterpretation of the findings in light of the recent research literature on automation transparency. In addition, the first author (Skraaning) was deeply involved in the planning and execution of Experiments 1 and 2 and served as principal investigator in Experiment 3. We relied heavily on the efforts of other researchers for the HAMMLAB data collection in all three experiments (see Acknowledgements).

## Experimental design.

Overview. Table 1 lists the independent variables and their levels of manipulation for Experiments 1 and 2. For this article, we consider only the automation transparency manipulation, which is described in detail in the following. Descriptions of the other independent variables are included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website). There were no main effects or interactions of these variables that are relevant to automation transparency.

Automation transparency manipulation. Expanding on the second row of Table 1, the transparent automation interface provided the operators with explicit verbal and visual information about automation activities (see Skjerve, Strand, Saarni, & Skraaning, 2002, pp. 25–28), which included the following:

• Key automatic devices presented on a large-screen overview display where operators could follow automation activity in real time. Automatic features were located next to their corresponding components/systems; for example, the status of turbine start-up/shutdown programs and controllers was inserted in the process mimic close to the graphical representation of the turbines (see Figure 2).

• Dedicated displays for detailed monitoring of controllers and automatic programs.

• Computer-based logic diagrams for tracking of automation sequences.

Table 1: Independent Variables and Their Levels of Manipulation in Experiments 1 and 2

| Independent Variable | Levels of Manipulation |
| --- | --- |
| Automation transparency | Transparent, traditional (see details in the following) |
| Operator role | Reactor operator (RO), turbine operator (TO), shift supervisor (SS)-only in Experiment 2 |
| Automation malfunction | Automation slips, automation mistakes |
| Scenario period | Early, mid, late |

Verbal feedback about the activity of automatic systems announced through loudspeakers and synchronized with visual feedback from automation (on the large-screen overview and controller displays). Details of that feedback differed by Experiment:

○ In Experiment 1, verbal feedback was given every time automatic devices started or failed (including routine work), with the same male voice for both the reactor and turbine side of the plant. The information was limited to behavioral feedback from automation (e.g., “program [name] starting up”), and announcements were repeated when automation reengaged multiple times around threshold values.

In Experiment 2, verbal feedback was provided only when the executive automatic programs started or automatic devices failed. We used a female voice on the reactor side and a male voice on the turbine side of the plant. The feedback from automation was both behavioral and diagnostic (e.g., “program [name] starting up due to [reason]”), and we constrained the feedback to a single announcement when automation reengaged multiple times around threshold values.

When working with the traditional automation interface, operators received no explicit visual or verbal feedback about automation responsibilities, capabilities, goals, activities, and/or effects. They had to infer these attributes of automation from changes in the plant process as reflected in a conventional HSI for supervisory control. Making such inferences is what the operators do in the normal course of their work, so we based the traditional automation interface on the prevailing industry practice for HAI. The operators had access to paper-based logic diagrams for tracking of automation sequences.

Test and simulation environment. Experiments 1 and 2 employed the Nokia Research Simulator (NORS) in HAMMLAB (Skjerve & Bye, 2011), a research facility for experimental studies of human performance in nuclear process control. A description of HAMMLAB is included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website). NORS represents a Russian water–water energetic reactor (VVER; see Skjerve, Andresen, Saarni, & Skraaning, 2001). The fully computerized control room established in HAMMLAB had separate workstations for the reactor and turbine side of the plant with eight 24″ displays arranged in two rows per workstation. A 2.00 × 0.75 m large-screen overview display was positioned between the workstations (see Figure 3). The experimental staff and data collection systems were located in an observation gallery separated from the control room by a glass wall.

The automatic features of NORS included interlocks, controllers, limitations, protections, and 130 available programs. Table 2 provides descriptions of the functions of each of these (see Skjerve et al., 2001, pp. 26–27, for a full description). These automatic systems had a local, subordinate, and inherent technical purpose directed toward plant components and systems but were not designed to take active control of the whole plant, like reactor protection systems or computerized operator procedure systems (IEEE 1786-2011, 2011). Hence, Experiments 1 and 2 investigated transparent automation on the component level of the plant.

The test scenarios ran for approximately 60 min each (excluding breaks between scenario periods) and emulated realistic NPP disturbances (Skjerve et al., 2001, pp. 35–39; Skjerve et al., 2002, pp. 48–54). The scenarios were developed by subject matter experts (SMEs) with decades of operational experience from the simulated plant. We ran four different scenarios per experiment, typically starting with a sequence of minor transients (like a leakage in the sealing water system for the reactor coolant pumps or failure of the controller for the pressurizer) leading up to more serious events toward the end of the scenario (such as a faulty steam generator feedwater line or failure in the restrictions from feedwater pumps). If the operators failed to take corrective actions, the situation escalated and resulted in manual or automatic reactor shutdown.

Participants and training. The participants were licensed NPP operators from the simulated plant. Experiment 1 tested 8 crews of two operators with a reactor operator (RO) and turbine operator (TO) in each crew. All 16 participants were male with an average age of 45.1 years (SD = 9.4 years, min = 29 years, max = 58 years). The participants’ average work experience as NPP operators was 12.2 years (SD = 8.6 years, min = 0.5 years, max = 23 years). Experiment 2 tested six crews of three operators with an RO, TO, and shift supervisor (SS) in each crew. The average age of the 18 participants was 41.8 years (SD = 8.9 years, min = 30 years, max = 56 years). All participants were male and their average work experience as control room operators was 11.2 years (SD = 7.9 years, min = 0 years, max = 24 years).

The participant training program lasted for 1½ days including a test scenario and covered (1) traditional and transparent automation displays, (2) other unfamiliar HSI features, and (3) differences between the operators’ home plant and the simulated process model.

## Human performance measurement.

Response time. The response time indicator measured the time from the annunciation of an anomaly in the process (e.g., an alarmed leakage) until the operators initiated fault-resolution actions (e.g., by isolating the leakage; see Skraaning, 2003, pp. 60–64). To compare responses to various events within and across scenarios, raw response times measured in minutes and seconds were transformed to standard scores (z-scores; Skraaning, 2003). To facilitate the interpretation of graphical effect illustrations across measures and studies, we inverted the scale, that is, higher z-scores mean that the operators responded more quickly to process events. Response times are inherently difficult to interpret (Skraaning, 2003) but are usually taken as an indicator of performance efficiency.

Task performance. The participants’ overall task performance in the test scenarios was measured with the Operator Performance Assessment System (OPAS; see Fernandes & Braarud, 2015; Lau, Jamieson, & Skraaning, 2016a; Skraaning, 1998, 2003, pp. 56–60; Skraaning et al., 2010, pp. 20–22; Skraaning et al., 2007, pp. 32–36). OPAS reveals the extent to which operators work in accordance with ideal scenario solutions prescribed a priori by SMEs who created the scenarios. The task elements are organized hierarchically according to scenario goals and weighted with respect to their importance for solving the scenario. The assessment is based on a combination of realtime observation from the experimenters’ gallery and retrospective analysis of recorded data. Further details on OPAS are provided (Supplemental Digital Material is available with the manuscript on the HF website). Two OPAS subscales were included: OPAS detections and operations. OPAS detections include the operators’ passive registration of process deviations, for example, through the alarm system, whereas OPAS operations comprise intervening actions, organizationally motivated activities (e.g., to declare emergency), information gathering, verification of process information, or other behaviors related to the task execution (see Skraaning, 1998, p. 17).

Human–automation cooperation. Human– automation cooperation was measured on a self-rating scale, where the participants evaluated the degree of collaborative support offered by automation in the test scenarios (Skjerve & Skraaning, 2004). For example, one item was “To what extent did automation provide relevant information about its activities? (1 = no relevant information; 7 = all relevant information).” The operators responded to six items on a 7-point visual analog scale. Scale items are included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website). The overall human–automation cooperation score was the unweighted average of all six items. A higher score indicated that the participants experienced better cooperation with automation. The human– automation cooperation scale was administered after each of the four test scenarios in Experiment 1 and after each of the three scenario periods in Experiment 2 (see Table 1).

Trust in automation. We employed a trust in automation scale (Strand, 2001). The participants responded to nine items on a 7-point visual analog scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. For example, one item was, “I know what the automatic system will do in the next 3 minutes.” The overall trust in automation score was the unweighted average of all nine items. A higher score meant that the operators had more trust in automation. Scale items are included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website). The trust scale was administered after each of the three scenario periods in Experiments 1 and 2 (see Table 1).

Workload. Perceived Task Complexity (Braarud, 1998, 2000; Lau et al., 2016a) served as the workload indicator. We presented five workload items on a 7-point visual analog scale ranging from 1 = very easy to 7 = very difficult. Scale items are included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website). For example, one item asked, “How difficult do you evaluate the current scenario to be in terms of . . . Identifying the cause(s) of the symptoms.” The overall workload score was the unweighted average of all five items. A higher score corresponded to higher levels of perceived workload. In nuclear process control settings, this instrument has demonstrated far better predictive validity across scenarios and experiments than NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX; see Braarud & Brendryen, 2001). The workload scale was administered after each of the three scenario periods in Experiments 1 and 2 (see Table 1).

SA. SA was assessed with the threedimensional (3D) version of the Situational Awareness Rating Technique (SART; Taylor, 1990). The short version of the scale was pre-ferred to limit the total number of items administered to the participants. Three items pertaining to attentional supply, attentional demand, and situation understanding were presented to the participants on a 7-point visual analog scale. Scale items are included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website). The overall SA score was calculated according to the standard formula for SART: SA = Situation understanding − (Attentional demand − Attentional Supply). The SA scale was administered after each of the three scenario periods in Experiments 1 and 2.

Statistical analysis model. The exact experimental design and statistical analysis model varied with the data aggregation procedures for each test, which could either be per crew or operator role, or per full scenario, or scenario period. The chosen level of data aggregation depended on the nature of the performance measure (e.g., task performance is usually measured for the whole crew over the full length of the scenario, whereas SA is typically measured per individual operator serving in an operator role and per scenario period). For all statistical tests, we defined completely crossed Randomized Block Factorial (RBF) designs based on repeated measurement or matching of crew members (Kirk, 1995) and analyzed the data with General Linear Model (GLM) software (Dell Inc., 2015). Counterbalancing procedures were employed to compensate for order effects (learning, fatigue, and carry-over effects) due to repeated exposure of the same participants to multiple test scenarios and experimental conditions (Skraaning, 2003, pp. 37–44).

In Experiment 1, the independent variables included in the statistical analysis model for the Response time and Task performance indicators were (1) Automation Transparency (Traditional vs. Transparent interface) as a within-subject factor and (2) Automation Malfunction (Automation slips vs. Automation mistakes) as a within-subject factor, that is, an RBF-22 design (see Kirk, 1995, pp. 454–455). For the human– automation cooperation scale, the independent variables included in the model were (1) Automation Transparency (Traditional vs. Transparent interface) as a within-subject factor, (2) Automation Malfunction (Automation slips vs. Automation mistakes) as a within-subject factor, and (3) Operator Role (RO and TO) through matching of operator roles per crew, that is, an RBF-222 design. For the trust in automation, workload, and SA scales, the independent variables included in the model were (1) Automation Transparency (Traditional vs. Transparent interface) as a within-subject factor, (2) Automation Malfunction (Automation slips vs. Automation mistakes) as a within-subject factor, (3) Operator Role (RO and TO) through matching of operator roles per crew, and (4) Scenario Period (Early, Mid, or Late disturbance) as a within-subject factor, that is, an RBF-2223 design.

In Experiment 2, the independent variables included in the statistical analysis model for the Response time and Task performance/OPAS detections indicators were (1) Automation Transparency (Traditional vs. Transparent interface) as a within-subject factor, (2) Automation Malfunction (Automation slips vs. Automation mistakes) as a within-subject factor, and (3) Scenario Period (Early, Mid, or Late disturbance) as a within-subject factor, that is, an RBF-223 design. For the Task performance/OPAS operations indicator, the independent variables included in the model were (1) Automation Transparency (Traditional vs. Transparent interface) as a within-subject factor and (2) Automation Malfunction (Automation slips vs. Automation mistakes) as a within-subject factor, that is, an RBF-22 design. For the human–automation cooperation, trust in automation, workload, and SA scales, the independent variables included in the model were (1) Automation Transparency (Traditional vs. Transparent interface) as a within-subject factor, (2) Automation Malfunction (Automation slips vs. Automation mistakes) as a within-subject factor, (3) Operator Role (RO, TO, and SS) through matching of operator roles per crew, and (4) Scenario Period (Early,

Mid, or Late disturbance) as a within-subject factor, that is, an RBF-2233 design.

## Results and Discussion

Psychometric analysis and statistical assumptions. We followed the typical analysis approach for simulator experiments in HAM-MLAB (see Skraaning, 2016, pp. 3, 23–27). This includes adopting classical experimental designs but rejecting null hypothesis significance testing as a meaningless mechanistic exercise. Rather, statistical analysis is used inductively to seek out robust patterns of results. The observed p value (ranging from $p = . 0 0$ to $p   =   1 . 0 0 )$ has a straightforward interpretation and serves as a direct indicator of statistical significance in our analyses, without the introduction of dichotomous accept–reject decisions with a predefined significance level. We report confidence intervals to assess uncertainties of sample means for all principal effects but avoid graphical presentation of these for withinsubject effects (Belia, Fidler, Williams, & Cumming, 2005). Effect sizes are presented for primary results in support of practical significance determination and future meta-analysis. However, these are interpreted in light of known limitations to comparison across measures and experiments, as well as susceptibility to the subjective judgment of the experimenter (Fern & Monroe, 1996). Finally, we seek to balance the risks of making false discoveries and inefficiency in exploring large datasets. Our strategy in striking this balance is to search for clear and consistent patterns of results that are corroborated through triangulation of evidence and supported by theory, previous experimental results, and practical experience. Further details about these and other analysis approaches adopted in HAMMLAB are provided ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website).

The human performance measures selected for the experiments were psychometrically evaluated, either in previous HAMMLAB studies and/or as reported in the methodological literature. Whenever possible, the sensitivity and inter-item reliability of the self-rating scales were assessed in the current data sets, seeking a Cronbach’s alpha >.80. We found all of the selected measures to be psychometrically acceptable. We did not detect any threats to the statistical conclusion validity of the experiments.

RIME figures for Experiments 1 and 2. Figures 4 and 5 present Results Integration across Measures and Experiments (RIME) figures for Experiments 1 and 2, respectively. Jamieson and Skraaning (2019) introduced RIME to provide integrative summaries of measures and their interpretation, independent variables in statistical models and data aggregation practices, statistical results, direction of effects, and the researchers’ concise holistic interpretations of results. The RIME figures presented here reflect an iteration of these results’ presentation format. Our ambition with RIME is to develop a concise, complete, compact, and readerfriendly format for reporting of experimental methods and results that complies with and fulfills the intentions behind the Publication Manual of the APA (2017). The most novel and salient feature of RIME is the final “Interpreted Support” column, which consists of one or two horizontal bars depicting the researchers’ judgment regarding the robustness and impact of the test result (based on p values, effect sizes, interval estimates, and the direction of the effect or pattern of interaction). The intent here is to put the statistical evidence (in the four columns to the left) and its interpretation (in the rightmost column) in close proximity to one another, thereby encouraging scrutiny of the researchers’ claims. A detailed explanation of the content and formatting of RIME is included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website).

As shown in Figures 4 and 5, the automation transparency manipulation produced clear and unambiguous results. As anticipated by the human factors literature, the transparent automation interface had a positive impact on human performance across measures. In Experiment 1, crews in the transparent automation condition responded to disturbances more quickly, exhibited superior task performance, reported better interaction with the automation, and experienced lower workload as compared to those using the traditional interface. The effects were even stronger and most consistent in Experiment 2 (Figure 4) after improving the content, sensitivity, and specificity of the automation feedback in response to operator input from Experiment 1 (Figure 5). Here, in addition to repeating the effects observed in Experiment 1, crews in the transparent automation condition also reported greater trust in the automation and demonstrated better SA.

It seems reasonable to interpret these results as providing substantial support for the automation transparency principle. The findings may even lead us to speculate that Norman (1990) was right in saying that “the problem is not automation, it is lack of feedback” (p. 4). Perhaps humans could operate highly automated systems with proficiency and ease if they were given sufficient feedback from automation.

## Experiment 3

Whereas Experiments 1 and 2 dealt with automation that is familiar to contemporary NPP operators, Experiment 3 investigated the effects of automation transparency for automation functionality that humans are likely to collaborate with in future plants. We are not suggesting that local automation at the component level (interlocks, controllers, limitations, protections, etc.) will become operationally irrelevant, but that operators are likely to become more engaged with agent-oriented automatic systems that achieve plant-wide goals. Thus, we shifted focus from automatic control features for components and technical systems to plant-wide procedure automation that can execute goaldriven taskwork that was previously carried out by humans, such as running up or shutting down the nuclear plant.

In Experiment 3, operators interacted with automatic systems that started up the simulated plant according to the operating procedures. The collaboration between humans and automation alluded to a teamwork metaphor (Christoffersen & Woods, 2002; Skjerve et al., 2005) where operators interacted with procedure automation agents. This metaphor was reflected in the transparent automation interface (see in the following).

## Method

A full-scope simulator study again tested the human performance of licensed operators in supervisory control of automated operational control tasks on a familiar nuclear plant.

## Experimental design.

Overview. Table 3 lists the independent variables and their levels of manipulation for Experiment 3. Similar to Experiments 1 and 2, we deal primarily with the automation transparency manipulation even though interactions with the other independent variables will inform our reasoning. The transparent and traditional interfaces are described in detail in the following. Definitions of the other independent variables are included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website).

Automation transparency manipulation. As in Experiments 1 and 2, we compared a transparent automation interface to a traditional automation interface. The transparent automation interface developed for Experiment 3 followed the same design principle as in Experiments 1 and 2, that is, we made the responsibilities, capabilities, goals, activities, and/or effects of automation directly observable in the user interface. However, the practical implementation of the principle had to be drastically different due to the focus on plant-wide procedure automation rather than local automation at the component level. For example, automatic procedure execution could not be distributed throughout the HSI but required a centralized presentation in the control room to make it possible for operators to follow the progression of automated taskwork.

Transparent automation interface. The transparent automation interface was presented on two adjacent $3 0 ^ { \prime \prime }$ computer screens (see Figure 6). The left screen served as an automation overview display, whereas the right screen constituted a detailed automation display. Both displays were included on workstations for crew members that interacted with procedure automation and intervened with the plant. Operators in a managerial role only had access to the automation overview display.

Automation overview display. The automation overview display had four circles with multiple sectors to monitor plant status. The sectors in each circle represented steps that had to be completed to reach overall goals in the plant start-up process. Sectors and circles went from green to blue as procedure steps were automatically executed and the goals reached, for example, automation could finish the eight steps in the left circle to make the reactor available. Red indicators on a sector (see Figure 6) alerted technical problems in a step. Thus, operators could monitor the progress as procedure automation started up the plant. Under the circles, there was a detailed list of actions that had been completed by automation in the ongoing step. Buttons for interaction with automation were placed above the circles. Operators could (1) set the plant in fully automatic mode (“auto” button), (2) resume automatic mode if the taskwork had paused due to technical failures (“återuppta” button), or (3) take over at any time and operate the plant manually (“hand” button).

Detailed automation display. The detailed automation display presented all historical and ongoing automation activities, both in chronological lists and graphical form. The graphics included animated overlays of the process mimic showing what automation was currently working on. When preconditions in the start-up procedures could not be fulfilled, automation had to pause and a red triangle over the process mimic suggested the location of the technical failure.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 6. Transparent automation displays (within the red rectangle): Automation overview display (left screen) and detailed automation display (right screen). Cutouts from automation overview display: Interaction buttons (on top) and Procedure step circle (to the right).

Traditional automation interface. In the traditional automation interface (Figure 7), we did not present any explicit information about the activities of the plant-wide procedure automation. Operators had to make inferences about automation activity based on process events and changes to system states, for example, through the overview display and/or process formats. Thus, neither of the two specialized automation displays (Figure 6) was presented to the operators in the traditional interface condition. This is how operators work normally, so we based the traditional automation interface on current industry standards for HAI design. A simple interface for interaction with automation was available in the traditional automation interface. The interaction buttons were functionally identical to the interaction buttons in the transparent automation interface (“auto,” “återuppta,” “hand”; as described earlier).

Test and simulation environment. Like Experiments 1 and 2, Experiment 3 was conducted in HAMMLAB. However, the process simulation employed was the HAMMLAB boiling water reactor simulator (HAMBO), representing a Swedish BWR plant (see Skraaning et al., 2010, p. 11). The fully computerized control room had separate workstations for the reactor and turbine side of the plant with a single row of 30″ liquid-crystal display (LCD) screens. There were three to six active screens per workstation depending on the experimental condition. A separate workstation for operators in a managerial role was placed behind the other two workstations. This station had two to four active screens depending on the experimental condition. A large-screen overview display was placed in front of the control room (see Figure 8).

In this experiment, automation followed computer scripts that performed operating procedures to bring the plant from cold start-up to 50% reactor power. The automatic system was organized as a synchronized ensemble of reactor, turbine, and supervisor agents that executed procedures and monitored for process deviations. The automation can be characterized as self-governed, effective, accurate, and highly active, but relatively unintelligent (similar to three coordinated washing machines). The automatic procedure execution paused when preconditions were not met, for example, due to technical failures, which was a typical event in the test scenarios. In such situations, the operators had to intervene in one of the following ways:

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 7. The traditional automation interface.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 8. HAMMLAB control room setup for Experiment 3.

• resolve technical failures first and then restart automation,

restart automation first and then deal with technical failures while automation continued to run up the plant,

• restart automation and ignore the technical failures (might be appropriate in many situations),

• continue to run up the plant manually and resolve technical failures in parallel, or

• shut down the plant for safety reasons.

We conducted eight realistic test scenarios that ran for approximately 35 min each (excluding the break between scenario periods). The scenarios covered different phases of plant start-up from cold shutdown to 50% reactor power. In the first phase of the scenarios, procedure automation was interrupted and paused due to technical failures, for example, unexpected pump stops, valve failures, or leakages. The crews had to handle the problem as suggested previously. The situation would then develop into a more complicated event with multiple failures that challenged the HAI (such as a high bearing temperature for a condensate pump combined with low differential pressure in the seal oil system for the generator and a faulty regulating valve for seal steam pressure). All scenarios were developed by SMEs.

Participants and training. The participants in Experiment 3 were licensed NPP operators from three Swedish plants based on a process model similar to HAMBO. We tested nine crews of three operators (i.e., 27 participants: 26 males and 1 female). The operators’ average age was 45.3 years (SD = 9.9 years, min = 27 years, max = 63 years), whereas the average work experience as a control room operator was 13.3 years (SD = 11.4 years, min = 0 years, max = 38 years).

The participant training program lasted for 1½ days including a test scenario and covered: (1) plant-wide procedure automation, (2) HAM-MLAB HSIs and transparent automation displays, and (3) differences between the home plant and the simulated process model.

Human performance measurement. The following human performance measures were used in Experiment 3:

Task performance. As in Experiments 1 and 2, we relied on OPAS as the indicator of task performance. As before, we calculated separate OPAS scores for detections and operations.

Self-rated task performance. The participants responded individually to a self-rated task performance scale developed specifically for nuclear process control. This scale was created in collaboration with experts on NPP operation and had been tested successfully in a previous HAM-MLAB experiment (see Skraaning et al., 2007). The participants rated nine items on a 5-point visual analog scale ranging from 1 = disagree to 5 = agree. For example, participants indicated their agreement with the statement, “I made correct diagnoses.” The self-rated task performance score was the unweighted average of all nine items. A higher score corresponded to higher levels of perceived task performance. Scale items are included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website). The self-rated task performance scale was administered after each of the two scenario periods in all eight scenarios (see Table 3).

SA. The Process Overview measure (Lau et al., 2016a, 2016b; Lau, Skraaning, Eitrheim, et al., 2011; Lau, Skraaning, Karlsson, Nihlwing, & Jamieson, 2011) captured participant

SA. This instrument can be seen as an adaptation and further development of the Situation Awareness Global Assessment Technique (SAGAT; Endsley, 2000) to support SA measurement in nuclear process control.

The Process Overview measure compares (1) the participants’ individual judgment of whether operationally relevant process parameters decreased, remained stable, or increased in the scenario period, with (2) the actual evolution of the process parameters in the same period. A sample item from Experiment 3 would be “Recently, the feedwater temperature before valve 312VC1 has (1) decreased, (2) remained stable, and (3) increased.” Discrepancies between the operators’ assessment and the actual process development indicated poor SA. When the participants rated the fluctuation of process parameters, we had temporarily frozen the simulator and blacked out all displays in the control room. The participants therefore needed to be cognitively aware of the process situation to respond correctly. Examples of Process Overview items are included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website). The proportion of correct operator responses reflected the individual level of SA. A higher score indicated better awareness. The self-rated task performance scale was administered after each of the two scenario periods in all eight scenarios (see Table 3).

Workload. As in Experiments 1 and 2, we relied on Perceived Task Complexity as the indicator of workload. The workload scale was administered after each of the two scenario periods (see Table 3).

Trust in automation. Trust in automation was measured with a slightly modified version of the scale used in Experiments 1 and 2. The participants responded to seven items on a 7-point visual analog scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. The overall trust in automation score was the unweighted average of all seven items. A higher score means that the operators had more trust in automation. Scale items are included ([Supplemental Digital Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0018720819887252) is available with the manuscript on the HF website). The trust in automation scale was administered after each of the two scenario periods in all eight scenarios (see Table 3).

Statistical analysis model. As in Experiments 1 and 2, the exact experimental design and statistical analysis model depended on the data aggregation procedures for each test. As before, we defined RBF designs based on repeated measurement or matching of crew members (Kirk, 1995) and analyzed the data with GLM (Dell Inc., 2015). Counterbalancing procedures were employed to compensate for order effects (learning, fatigue, carry-over effects) due to repeated exposure of the same participants to multiple test scenarios and experimental conditions (Skraaning, 2003, pp. 37–44).

In Experiment 3, the independent variables included in the statistical analysis model for the Task performance indicators (OPAS detections and OPAS operations) and the Self-rated task performance scale were (1) Automation Transparency (Traditional vs. Transparent interface) as a within-subject factor, (2) Staffing Solution (Conventional single unit vs. Experimental multi unit) as a within-subject factor, (3) Overview Display (Mimic based vs. Configural graphics) as a within-subject factor, and (4) Scenario Period (Easy vs. Difficult phase) as a within-subject factor, that is, an RBF-2222 design (see Kirk, 1995, pp. 454–455). For the SA indicator and the Workload and Trust in automation scales, the independent variables included in the model were (1) Automation Transparency (Traditional vs. Transparent interface) as a within-subject factor, (2) Overview Display (Mimic based vs. Configural graphics) as a within-subject factor, (3) Scenario Period (Easy vs. Difficult phase) as a within-subject factor, and (4) Operator Role (RO, TO, and MO) through matching of operator roles per crew, that is, an RBF-2223 design.

## Results and Discussion

Psychometric analysis and statistical assumptions. As in Experiments 1 and 2, we continued to follow the typical analysis approach for simulator experiments in HAM-MLAB. All performance measures were judged to be psychometrically acceptable and we did not detect any threats to the statistical conclusion validity of the experiment.

RIME figure. Figure 9 shows the RIME figure for Experiment 3.

In contrast to Experiments 1 and 2, Figure 9 reveals inconsistent and contradictory human performance responses to the automation transparency manipulation. Of greatest concern, the operators’ detection of deviating process states (OPAS detections) was negatively affected by the transparent automation displays. We were also surprised by the unconvincing effect on the operators’ active task performance (OPAS operations). Automation transparency had an impact on the participants’ self-rated task performance, but in opposite directions depending on the staffing solution. For SA, the effect of the transparent automation manipulation was moderated by the type of overview display that operators worked with and the scenario period. The effect of automation transparency on workload depended on the operator role. Trust in automation was the only measure that produced a main effect similar to Experiments 1 and 2. Although we could discuss these results in detail, the focus of this article is on the consistency of the evidence in support of automation transparency across different applications of the design principle. It is therefore sufficient to expose here that the clear and unambiguous results from Experiments 1 and 2 were lost in Experiment 3.

## Integrated Discussion of The Automation Transparency Studies

The contrasts between Figures 4 and 5 for Experiments 1 and 2, respectively, and Figure 9 for Experiment 3 are striking. The clear and strong advantages of automation transparency that we observed in Experiments 1 and 2 were absent from Experiment 3.

## Methodological Differences Between Experiments

A ready explanation for the surprising results of Experiment 3 could be that the anomalous results are attributable to variations in the method. For example,

• Operators were more familiar with the dutiful automation employed in Experiments 1 and 2 as

compared to the agent-like automation employed in Experiment 3.

HAMMLAB was modernized and enlarged after Experiments 1 and 2 (cf. Figures 3 and 8).

Experiment 3 was performed on a BWR simulator with Swedish operators as participants, whereas Experiments 1 and 2 used a VVER simulator with Finnish participants.

• The research and design team was composed differently in the experiments.

The experimental methodology evolved in the period between the experiments, resulting, for example, in slightly modified performance measures and data collection techniques.

However, all experiments were full-scope simulator experiments with licensed NPP operators as participants. We employed similar methods originating from the same research culture with several common staff members involved. From this perspective, it seems unlikely that variations in method can explain the discrepancies. If they could, this would cast doubt on the fitness of the automation transparency principle. A robust design principle should not be challenged by differences between plants, operator populations, laboratory environments, or even industry domains. We have to assume that providing feedback from automation will produce superior human performance across a wide range of operating conditions. Otherwise, the transparent automation principle would be diluted and its generalizability undermined. Given the presumed generic value of the principle, it is therefore unreasonable to explain the findings of Experiment 3 by pointing to variations in the method.

## Implementation of Automation and the Automation Transparency Principle

More plausible explanations for the lack of support for the automation transparency principle in Experiment 3 might be found in the combined effects of the agent-like procedure automation and the accompanying design of the transparent automation displays:

Operators may have had insufficient capacity to simultaneously monitor procedure automation and detect deviating process states. According to this explanation, the monitoring and interaction with plant-wide automation through centralized displays in the control room is more demanding than handling local automation at the component level of the plant. The operators’ spare capacity to detect process deviations may therefore have suffered in Experiment 3. With an increasing focus on supervising automation rather than monitoring the plant, the transparency of plant-wide procedure automation may indirectly have changed the operator role.

The transparent automation interface may have attracted too much attention. The novel nature of the transparent automation displays in Experiment 3 may have diverted the operators’ attention away from alarms and other process information.

Operators may have paid extra attention to the process state when working through the traditional automation interface. When the participants worked with the traditional automation interface in Experiment 3, they had to infer automation activity from process events and fluctuations of plant parameters. The only way to achieve this was through the traditional displays, which supported tracking of process information in parallel.

This may have given the traditional automation interface an advantage when it comes to detection of deviating process states. In Experiments 1 and 2, the transparent automation elements were interlocks, controllers, limitations, protections, and programs positioned close to the local process functions that they controlled. In that case, the traditional automation interface had no special advantages over the transparent automation interface for monitoring of process information.

A common insight across these explanations is that the transparency of plant-wide procedure automation may be difficult to realize without implicitly changing the operational concept (operator roles, responsibilities, task allocation, teamwork, work practices, etc.). To make plant-wide procedure automation transparent, we may have inadvertently introduced dysfunctional features to the operational concept and thereby eliminated the human performance benefits of transparency. Whereas the transparency principle may fit readily into the operational concept for local automation at the component level—and yield clear benefits—its implementation for plant-wide procedure automation may force unplanned changes to the operational concept and result in failure to obtain the expected benefits.

## Other Implementations of the Automation Transparency Principle

These results encourage consideration of other efforts to generalize the benefits of automation transparency to new operational settings. In studies sharing an emphasis on agent-oriented automation with Experiment 3, Mercado et al. (2016) and Stowers et al. (2016) investigated the effects of agent transparency for planning of unmanned vehicle operations. They compared three graded implementations of agent transparency, with more levels expected to improve task performance, enhance SA, decrease workload, and engender appropriate trust in the agent. The support for the transparency principle from these studies is far from convincing. The effects on performance accuracy seem solid (Mercado et al., 2016; Stowers et al., 2016), but the hypothesized effects on operator workload were statistically insignificant (Chen et al., 2018; Mercado et al., 2016), and the reported effects on trust were restricted to certain subscales of trust and selected blocks of data (Mercado et al., 2016). Stowers et al. (2016) reported that “response time significantly increased with increased transparency, suggesting that operators were spending a longer time reading and processing information portrayed in the higher transparency conditions” (Chen et al., 2018, p. 268), suggesting a speed–accuracy trade-off (Heitz, 2014). Finally, neither of the two studies reported any tests of SA. In a similar study of agent-oriented automation, Selkowitz et al. (2016) demonstrated compelling effects of transparency on trust, but the effects on workload and SA were statistically insignificant and weak. Finally, Wright et al. (2016) reported statistically insignificant and weak effects of agent transparency for task performance and several workload indicators.

Considering these selected observations along with the outcome of Experiment 3, Norman’s (1990) hypothesis that “the problem is not automation, it is a lack of feedback” (p. 4) appears simplistic. In the words of Christoffersen and Woods (2002),

Providing effective feedback to operators in complex, highly automated environments represents a significant challenge to which there are no ready-made solutions. Answering this challenge for the current and future generations of automation will require fundamentally new approaches to designing representations of automation activity. (p. 6)

Providing feedback to operators is obviously not a ready-made solution for all implementations of automation. It may not even be advisable if the feedback from automation transforms the operational concept in unanticipated ways and distorts human performance as a consequence.

## Conclusion

Based on the outcome of Experiments 1 and 2, we are confident that operators should be provided with more explicit feedback from automation than what is typically made available. Such feedback seems to improve most aspects of human performance for local automation at the component level of the technical system. The question is whether the evidence for the positive effects of automation transparency can be generalized to other forms of automation. The results of Experiment 3 suggest that such generalizations may be problematic for plant-wide procedure automation. For this form of automation, the unambiguous positive effects of automation transparency that we observed in Experiments 1 and 2 were lost and the operators’ detection of deviating process states was impaired by introducing explicit feedback from automation. Similarly, findings from Mercado et al. (2016), Stowers et al. (2016), Selkowitz et al., (2016), and Wright et al. (2016) all fail to offer a strong endorsement of the transparency principle (beyond trust) and performance accuracy for other implementations of agent-based automation. These outcomes suggest that automation transparency may have surprising limits as a design principle and that overgeneralization of its benefits across operating contexts should be circumvented.

## Key Points

• The automation transparency design principle anticipates that making information about the responsibilities, capabilities, goals, activities, and/ or effects of automation observable in the HSI will yield more effective reliance, more appropriate trust, better understanding, and greater user satisfaction.

Two full-scope simulation studies provide strong evidence in support of the automation transparency principle when applied to automation at the component level of a nuclear process. A third full-scope simulation study failed to provide evidence in support of the automation transparency principles when applied to agent-like plant-wide procedure automation.

• The contrast in findings between the experiments is interpreted as evidence of a practical limitation to the application of automation transparency.

• Human factors practitioners should be mindful of the potential limitations of the principle in designing for human interaction with agent-oriented automation.

Gyrd Skraaning is a principal scientist at the Institute for Energy Technology (IFE) and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Halden Reactor Project. He received his PhD in experimental psychology from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in 2003.

Greg A. Jamieson is a professor and Clarice Chalmers Chair of Engineering Design at the University of Toronto. He received his PhD in mechanical and industrial engineering from the University of Toronto in 2003. He is a licensed professional engineer in Ontario.
